pablo-neruda: Ricardo Eliécer Neftalí Reyes Basoalto was born on 12 July 1904 in Parral, about 350 km south of Santiago. His father, José del Carmen Reyes Morales, was a railway employee. His mother, the schoolteacher Rosa Neftalí Basoalto Opazo, died two months after his birth. He grew up in Temuco and composed his first poems in the winter of 1914.

His father opposed his interest in literature, but others encouraged him, among them the future Nobel laureate Gabriela Mistral, who headed the local school. On 18 July 1917, aged 13, he published an essay in the daily La Mañana under the name Neftalí Reyes. By mid-1920 he had adopted the pseudonym Pablo Neruda and was a published author of poems, prose and journalism. He is thought to have taken the name from the Czech poet Jan Neruda.

Neruda held diplomatic posts in Buenos Aires and Barcelona, then succeeded Mistral as consul in Madrid, where he became the centre of a literary circle that included Rafael Alberti, Federico García Lorca and César Vallejo. He later served as Consul General in Mexico City from 1940 to 1943. Back in Chile in 1943, he toured Peru and visited Machu Picchu, which inspired the 12-part poem Alturas de Macchu Picchu, completed in 1945, and later Canto General (1950).

Like many left-leaning intellectuals of his generation, Neruda came to admire the Soviet Union of Joseph Stalin, and he received the Stalin Peace Prize in 1953. His friend Octavio Paz later criticised this loyalty. When President Gabriel González Videla outlawed communism in 1948, a warrant was issued for the Communist senator's arrest. Friends hid him for 13 months, and in March 1949 he crossed the Andes on horseback into Argentina. He returned to Chile in August 1952 to support Salvador Allende's presidential campaign.

Under President Allende, Neruda served as ambassador to France. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1971, though some committee members had not forgotten his praise of Stalinist dictatorship. In September 1973 he was diagnosed with prostate cancer, and after the coup led by Augusto Pinochet he planned to go into exile in Mexico. He died at a clinic in Santiago on 23 September 1973, the day before he was to leave. The official cause was complications of prostate cancer, but the circumstances of his death have been investigated since 2011.

Neruda is often considered the national poet of Chile. His three houses, La Chascona in Santiago, La Sebastiana in Valparaíso and Casa de Isla Negra, are museums, and he and Matilde Urrutia are buried at Isla Negra.
pablo-picasso: Pablo Ruiz Picasso was born on 25 October 1881 in Málaga, Andalusia, the first child of José Ruiz y Blasco and María Picasso y López. His father was a painter of birds and other game and a professor at the School of Crafts. According to his mother, his first word was "piz, piz", short for lápiz, the Spanish word for pencil. From the age of seven he was trained by his father, a traditional academic artist, in figure drawing and oil painting. The family moved to A Coruña in 1891, and an apocryphal story relates that his father, seeing the precision of the thirteen-year-old's technique, felt his son had surpassed him.

His career as a painter can be said to have begun by 1894. The academic realism of the mid-1890s appears in The First Communion (1896), and a Modernist period followed in 1899–1900. After 1906 the Fauvist work of Henri Matisse pushed him towards more radical styles, beginning a rivalry between the two. The commonly accepted periods are the Blue Period (1901–1904), the Rose Period (1904–1906), the African-influenced Period (1907–1909), Analytic Cubism (1909–1912) and Synthetic Cubism (1912–1919). His works include Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (1907) and Guernica (1937). From 1909 to 1928 he made sculptural constructions from diverse materials, such as Guitar (1912) in sheet metal and wire. In 1944 he joined the French Communist Party, and he remained a member until his death.

Picasso died on 8 April 1973 in Mougins, France, of a heart attack, having painted until 3 a.m. the night before. He died without a will, which led to a feud over his estate. At his death there were more than 45,000 unsold works in his estate, among them 1,885 paintings, 1,228 sculptures and 3,222 ceramics. In 1971 he was the first living artist honoured with an exhibition in the Grand Gallery of the Louvre, for his 90th birthday.
pacific-ocean: The Pacific is the largest and deepest of Earth's five oceanic divisions. It covers about 165,250,000 square kilometres, taking the definition with an Antarctic southern border, which is about 46% of Earth's water surface. Its mean depth is 4,000 metres, and the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, at 10,928 metres, is the deepest known point in the world. More than 25,000 islands rise above its surface, many of them the remains of volcanoes, and the Ring of Fire, a belt of explosive volcanism above subduction zones, surrounds it.

Modern humans first reached the western Pacific around 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. They crossed from Sundaland to Sahul, a sea journey of at least 80 kilometres, to reach Australia, probably on large bamboo rafts, although the level of maritime technology is not known with certainty. Settlement of Buka by 32,000 years ago and Manus by 25,000 years ago confirms their seafaring skill. Their descendants include the Negritos, Melanesians and Indigenous Australians.

In 1513 the Spanish explorer Vasco Núñez de Balboa crossed the Isthmus of Panama and sighted what he called the Mar del Sur, the Southern Sea. The present name was given by Ferdinand Magellan during the Spanish circumnavigation of 1520, when he met favourable winds and called it Mar Pacífico, the peaceful sea. From 1946 to 1958 the Marshall Islands served as the Pacific Proving Grounds designated by the United States, where 67 nuclear tests were conducted.

The Pacific is divided by the equator into the North and South Pacific. Its marginal seas include the Philippine Sea, the South China Sea, the East China Sea, the Sea of Japan, the Sea of Okhotsk, the Bering Sea, the Tasman Sea and the Coral Sea. The Bering Strait joins it to the Arctic Ocean, and the Drake Passage and Strait of Magellan link it to the Atlantic. It is the only ocean mostly bounded by subduction zones.
pakistan: Pakistan is bounded by the Arabian Sea on the south and shares land borders with India to the east, Afghanistan to the west, Iran to the southwest and China to the northeast. The Wakhan Corridor, a narrow strip of Afghanistan, separates it from Tajikistan. It lies where the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates meet, a region of high seismic activity.

The country is divided into three major geographic areas: the northern highlands, the Indus River plain and the Balochistan Plateau. The highlands include the Karakoram, Hindu Kush and Pamir ranges and five of the fourteen peaks over 8,000 metres, among them K2 at 8,611 metres. The 1,609 km Indus River and its tributaries cross the country from Kashmir to the Arabian Sea and sustain the alluvial plains of Punjab and Sindh.

The earliest known stone tools in the region, about 2 million years old, were found in the Soan Valley. The Neolithic site of Mehrgarh dates from 7000 to 4300 BCE, and the Indus Valley Civilisation included Mohenjo-daro and Harappa. After its decline, semi-nomadic Indo-European Aryans migrated into the subcontinent around 2000 BCE, and the Gandhara civilisation later flourished at the crossroads of India, Central Asia and the Middle East.

The western regions became part of the Achaemenid Empire around 517 BCE, and Alexander the Great conquered the region in 326 BCE, defeating King Porus at Jhelum. The Mauryas ruled from 322 BCE to 185 BCE, and Ashoka introduced Buddhism. The Indo-Greek Kingdom founded by Demetrius of Bactria included Gandhara and Punjab, and Greco-Buddhist culture flourished under Menander. Later powers included the Kushan, the Ghaznavids, the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals, and the British Raj from 1858 to 1947.

Pakistan gained independence in 1947 through the partition of British India, which was accompanied by mass migration and loss of life. It adopted a republican constitution in 1956, and East Pakistan seceded as Bangladesh in 1971 after a nine-month civil war. The 1973 constitution established a parliamentary system. Military rule governed in 1958 to 1971, 1977 to 1988 and 1999 to 2008, and the first successful democratic transition took place in May 2013.

The 2023 census counted 247,541,947 people, and the population grew more than sevenfold between 1951 and 2023. The country is ethnically and linguistically diverse and has a very young population, with a median age of 19. Its legislature has a 96-member Senate and a 336-member National Assembly.
palau: Palau is an archipelago of about 340 islands in the western Pacific Ocean, the western part of the Caroline Islands, with a total area of 466 square kilometres. Its most populous islands are Angaur, Babeldaob, Koror and Peleliu, and about two-thirds of the people live on Koror. North of them lies the coral atoll of Kayangel, and west lie about 200 uninhabited Rock Islands. A remote group of six Southwest Islands, some 604 kilometres away, make up the states of Hatohobei and Sonsorol.

The Palauan name for the islands, Belau, derives from the word for village, beluu, or from aibebelau, meaning indirect replies, which relates to a creation myth. The name Palau came into English from the Spanish Los Palaos through German. An older English name was the Pelew Islands.

The islands were first settled in the 3rd or 2nd millennium BCE by Austronesian peoples, most likely from what is now the Philippines or Indonesia. In December 1696 sailors from the Caroline Islands were stranded on Samar, where the missionary Paul Klein met them. They showed him with pebbles the position and size of their islands, and he drew from this the first European map of the Palau area.

The islands became part of the Spanish East Indies in 1885. After Spain's defeat in the Spanish-American War they were sold to Germany in 1899 and administered as part of German New Guinea. After the First World War they fell within the Japanese-ruled South Seas Mandate of the League of Nations. In the Second World War American and Japanese troops fought in the Mariana and Palau Islands campaign, including the major Battle of Peleliu.

In 1947 Palau became part of the United States-governed Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. A referendum in 1978 rejected joining the Federated States of Micronesia, and Palau adopted a constitution in 1981. It gained full sovereignty in 1994 under a Compact of Free Association with the United States, and the United Nations General Assembly admitted it on 15 December 1994.

The Republic of Palau is a presidential republic with a bicameral Palau National Congress. Its capital, Ngerulmud, is on Babeldaob, the largest island, and its most populous city is Koror. The official languages are Palauan and English, and the currency is the United States dollar. Palauan society follows a strict matrilineal system, seen in funerals, marriages, inheritance and the passing of traditional titles.
palermo: Palermo lies in a basin formed by the Papireto, Kemonia and Oreto rivers, which the Arabs named the Conca d'Oro, the Golden Basin, in the 9th century. A mountain range forms a cirque around the city and faces the Tyrrhenian Sea, and historically it made the interior of Sicily hard to reach. Monte Pellegrino, which stands apart in front of the sea, is the historically most important of the mountains, and Goethe called its cliff the most beautiful promontory in the world. Cave drawings at nearby Addaura show settlement perhaps around 8000 BCE.

The original inhabitants were the Sicani, who according to Thucydides arrived from the Iberian Peninsula. In the 8th century BCE the Phoenicians built a settlement on the natural harbour, one of their three main colonies in Sicily along with Motya and Soluntum, and the city later passed to Carthage. As Panormus it was part of the Roman Republic and Empire for over a thousand years. The Vandals under Geiseric took it in 440 CE, and in late 535 Belisarius laid siege to the city, which had refused to surrender, and eventually prevailed. From 831 to 1072 Palermo was under Arab rule and for the first time the capital of Sicily.

After the Norman conquest it became the capital of the Kingdom of Sicily, which lasted from 1130 to 1816. Spain ruled the city from 1479 until 1713, with brief interruptions, and Austria from 1720 to 1734. Charles III chose Palermo for his coronation as King of Sicily, but the royal court resided in Naples. In 1866 Palermo was the seat of a week-long popular rebellion against annexation by the Savoy kingdom, which was crushed under martial law, and the Teatro Massimo opened in 1897.

Allied bombing in 1942 and 1943 destroyed the harbour and much of the city, with heavy civilian casualties, until the Allied invasion of Sicily captured it on 22 July 1943. In 1946 Palermo became the seat of the Regional Parliament, and in 1948 the element technetium was discovered at its university.

Palermo is the capital and largest city of Sicily. Its inhabitants speak Italian and the Palermitano dialect of Sicilian. The city is the main seat of the World Heritage Site Arab-Norman Palermo and the Cathedral Churches of Cefalù and Monreale, and its markets of Vucciria, Ballarò and Capo are known for fruit, vegetables and fish. Its patron saint is Saint Rosalia, whose feast day is 15 July.
palk-strait: The strait stretches for about 137 km and is between 64 and 137 km wide. Its waters are shallow: around the shoals of Ram Setu they are typically only 1 to 3 metres deep, the central part is typically around 20 metres deep, and the greatest depth is 35 metres. To the north, in the Bay of Bengal, the waves are mostly swells, while in Palk Bay to the south they are mostly smaller wind waves. In the Hindu epic Ramayana the shoals are part of a bridge built by the vanara army of Rama to rescue his wife Sita from the Asura king Ravana.

During the Last Glacial Period, when sea levels fell to as much as 120 metres below their present values, the whole of the shallow strait was dry land. It was submerged again as the sea rose during the Holocene, by around 7,000 years ago.

The construction of a shipping channel through the strait was first proposed to the British government of India in 1860. Pamban Island was linked to the Indian mainland by the Pamban Bridge, opened for traffic on 24 February 1914. Trains ran from Madras to Dhanushkodi at the southern tip of the island, where a ferry crossed to Talaimannar on Mannar Island and another train carried passengers on to Colombo. The railway line to Dhanushkodi was destroyed in the 1964 Dhanushkodi cyclone together with a passenger train, killing around 200 people. A ferry between Rameswaram and Talaimannar continued into the 1970s and was discontinued by the Indian government in 1984.

The shallows, small islands and reefs make the strait difficult for large ships, though fishing boats and small craft navigate it. The Sethusamudram Shipping Canal Project, commissioned by the Government of India in 2005 to dredge a channel, met opposition on religious grounds. A road bridge beside the Pamban Bridge was opened in 1988, and a new railway bridge was completed in 2024 after rail traffic on the old bridge was suspended permanently in February 2023 over concerns about its stability. A combined undersea tunnel and bridge linking India and Sri Lanka, the Palk Strait Bridge, was first discussed in 2002 and has been examined several times since.
panama-canal: The idea of a canal across the Isthmus of Panama dates back to 1513, when the Spanish conquistador Vasco Núñez de Balboa first crossed the isthmus and noted the possibility in his journal. The earliest proposal for action dates to 1534, when the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V ordered a survey for a route through the Americas to ease the voyage of ships between Spain and Peru. In 1668 the English physician and philosopher Sir Thomas Browne proposed the isthmus as the most convenient place for such a canal.

The French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps, who had built the Suez Canal, and the engineer Philippe Bunau-Varilla led the French attempt, begun in 1881. A concession from the Colombian government, obtained in 1878 and valid for 99 years, allowed the company to dig and exploit a canal. The French stopped in 1889 because investors lost confidence after engineering problems and a high death rate among workers. The United States took control of the canal property on 4 May 1904, inheriting a depleted workforce and a mass of equipment, much of it in poor condition.

The canal is an artificial waterway 82 kilometres long that connects the Caribbean Sea with the Pacific Ocean at the narrowest point of the isthmus. Because of the shape of the isthmus its general direction from the Atlantic to the Pacific is from north-west to south-east. Locks at each end lift ships up to Gatun Lake, an artificial lake 26 metres above sea level, created in 1913 by damming the Chagres River; locks at the other end lower them again. At its creation Gatun Lake was the largest human-made lake in the world. The original locks are 33.5 metres wide and admit ships of the Panamax size. A third, wider set of locks, built between 2007 and 2016, takes larger vessels.

The United States built the canal under the Isthmian Canal Commission, which also controlled the Panama Canal Zone. In 1907 Stevens resigned as chief engineer and President Theodore Roosevelt appointed Major George Washington Goethals of the US Army Corps of Engineers, who finished the work in 1914, two years ahead of the target date. The canal opened on 15 August 1914.

It shortened voyages between the oceans and spared ships the long and hazardous route around the southern tip of South America. Traffic rose from about 1,000 ships in 1914 to 14,702 vessels in 2008. The United States kept control of the canal and the Panama Canal Zone until the Torrijos–Carter Treaties of 1977 provided for its handover to Panama. After a period of joint American and Panamanian control, the Panamanian government took over in 1999, and the canal is now run by the Panama Canal Authority.
pandara-vanniyan: Kulasegaram Vairamuthu Pandara Vanniyan was a native of the Vanni and is said to have reigned there from 1785. Much about his family is unclear, but reports give him a sister, Nallanachal Vanniyan, and two younger brothers who served as his minister and his commander. He married into the family of Kumarasinghe Maha Vanniya of Nuwara Wewa, and so gained political power in the southern Vanni as well as the north. He is said to have lived at Kumulamunai, in the present Mullaitivu District.

The Vanni served as a buffer zone between the north and south of Sri Lanka. After the Portuguese captured the Jaffna Kingdom in 1621 the region was under their nominal control, and around 1782 the Dutch defeated the Vanniar chieftains.

Pandara Vanniyan is said to have defeated the Dutch officer Lieutenant von Driberg several times. Against the British, the Vanniars carried on a predatory warfare in Mannar and Trincomalee and reached the Jaffna Peninsula, and the British built forts to keep them at bay. In alliance with the Kandy Kingdom he rose to expel the British from his district. On 25 August 1803 he attacked the Government House at Mullaitivu, drove out the garrison under Captain Edward Mudge of the 19th Regiment and seized the fort and its cannons. He then overran the northern districts as far as Elephant Pass.

He turned from conventional warfare to guerrilla tactics, but the British organised a three-pronged attack from Jaffna, Mannar and Trincomalee. Von Driberg, who had stayed on after the British ousted the Dutch, defeated him on 31 October 1803 at Katsilaimadu, capturing a cannon given to him by the Kandyan king Sri Wickrema Rajasinghe. His houses were burned and his people dispersed into the jungle and out of the Vanni.

No longer a ruler, Pandara Vanniyan withdrew to areas near the Kandy Kingdom. Accounts of his end differ: by one he died fighting the British, by another he remained there until September 1810, when British forces ambushed him, and later died of his injuries. Von Driberg set up a granite monument at Katsilaimadu recording the defeat; in 2010 it was found broken. Prime Minister Ranasinghe Premadasa declared him a national hero in 1982, and a statue stands in Vavuniya. Tamil nationalists honour him as an epic hero, and he is the subject of a novel by M. Karunanidhi and of a play by Mullaimani Ve Cuppiramaniyam that won a prize from the Ceylon Art Council in 1964.
papacy: According to Catholic tradition, the apostolic see of Rome was founded by Saint Peter and Saint Paul in the first century. The Catholic Church teaches that the bishop of Rome succeeded Saint Peter, to whom, in its reading of Matthew 16, Jesus gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the powers of binding and loosing. Cyprian of Carthage, in his Letter 55 of about 251 CE to Pope Cornelius, recognised the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor.

The word pope comes from the Greek páppas, father. In the early centuries it was applied, especially in the East, to all bishops and senior clergy. It became reserved in the West to the bishop of Rome during the reign of Leo I (440 to 461), though this was made official only in the 11th century.

In ancient times popes helped spread Christianity and intervened in doctrinal disputes. In the Middle Ages they played a role of secular importance in Western Europe, often arbitrating between Christian monarchs, and their influence eventually rivalled that of territorial rulers. From the 8th century until 1870 the pope was sovereign of the Papal States, and since the Lateran Treaty of 1929 he has headed the much smaller Vatican City State. Between 1309 and 1378 the popes lived in Avignon, France, a period often called the Babylonian captivity. The First Vatican Council defined the pope's authority on 18 July 1870, and in 1870 the dogma of papal infallibility was proclaimed for the rare occasions when the pope speaks ex cathedra on faith or morals.

The pope was originally chosen by the senior clergy in and near Rome. In 1059 the electorate was restricted to the cardinals, and in 1179 the votes of all cardinal electors were made equal. The last pope elected when not yet a bishop was Gregory XVI in 1831, and the last not a cardinal was Urban VI in 1378. Popes adopt a new name on accession.

His official seat is the Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran, and his residence the Apostolic Palace. Antipopes are claimants not canonically elected; briefly in the 15th century three separate lines of popes claimed authenticity. Eastern Orthodox churches and the Anglican Communion accept apostolic succession and a primacy of honour but reject the pope as Peter's successor in any other sense than other bishops.
papua-new-guinea: The country covers 462,840 km2 and includes a large mainland and hundreds of islands in Melanesia, north of Australia. It lies where the north-moving Indo-Australian plate meets the west-moving Pacific plate, which gives it a highly variable geography, active volcanoes and frequent earthquakes. Mountains cover at least 72% of the country, and the highest point is Mount Wilhelm, at 4,509 metres. The Torres Strait, 152 kilometres wide, separates it from Australia's Cape York Peninsula. This terrain helps explain why the population is largely rural and divided into many small communities.

Archaeological evidence indicates that modern humans first reached what became New Guinea around 42,000 to 45,000 years ago. Agriculture was developed independently in the New Guinea highlands around 7000 BCE, making it one of the few areas where people domesticated plants without outside influence. Austronesian-speaking peoples of the Lapita culture had reached the Bismarck Archipelago by about 3,300 years ago. Communities were linked by trade, and bananas and sugarcane probably passed from New Guinea to other regions along these networks, but each community otherwise functioned largely independently.

European names for the island date from the 16th century: Jorge de Menezes called it Ilhas dos Papuas in 1526, and Yñigo Ortiz de Retez named it Nueva Guinea in 1545. In 1884 the eastern half was divided between German New Guinea in the north and British New Guinea in the south. The British territory was ceded to Australia in 1902 and became the Territory of Papua. Australia occupied German New Guinea during the First World War and then ruled it as a League of Nations mandate. The two territories were united in 1949, after fierce fighting there in World War II, and the country became independent in 1975. Europeans brought together communities that had sometimes been hostile or had no relationship at all.

Papua New Guinea is a Commonwealth realm with a governor-general representing the monarch and a unicameral National Parliament of 118 seats, in a Westminster system. Its capital and largest city is Port Moresby. There are 840 known spoken languages, the most of any country, and English and Tok Pisin serve as common languages. Most people live in customary communities, and the constitution protects traditional communities and lifestyles.
paraguay: Paraguay lies between latitudes 19° and 28°S in the central region of South America and is divided by the Río Paraguay into two regions. The eastern region has mostly grassy plains and wooded hills, while the western region, known as the Chaco and part of the Gran Chaco, has mostly low, marshy plains. The far eastern forest belt receives an average of 170 centimetres of rain a year, the western Chaco no more than 50 centimetres. Although landlocked, Paraguay reaches the Atlantic Ocean by the Paraná–Paraguay Waterway, a system of navigable channels shared by five countries.

The Guaraní had lived in eastern Paraguay for at least a millennium when the Spanish arrived. The Gran Chaco in the west was inhabited by nomads, of whom the Guaycuru peoples were most prominent, and the Paraguay River roughly divided the agricultural Guaraní from them. The Mbayá were known for their warrior traditions and were not fully pacified until the late 19th century. Juan de Salazar de Espinosa founded Asunción on 15 August 1537, and it became the centre of the Spanish colonial province of Paraguay.

In the eighteenth century Jesuit missions developed reductions to gather Guaraní populations and protect them from virtual slavery by Spanish settlers and Portuguese slave raiders, the bandeirantes. The reducciones flourished in eastern Paraguay for about 150 years, until the Spanish Crown expelled the Jesuits in 1767. Paraguay overthrew the local Spanish administration on 14 May 1811. José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, nicknamed El Supremo, ruled from 1814 until his death in 1840 with very little outside contact, intending a utopian society based on Rousseau's Social Contract. The Triple Alliance War of 1864 to 1870 cost the country half its prewar population and around a quarter to a third of its territory. Paraguay then prevailed in the Chaco War with Bolivia of 1932 to 1935.

Asunción is the capital and largest city. Paraguay is a unitary presidential republic of seventeen departments and a capital district. The population was 6,109,944 at the 2022 census, and most people live in the east. Paraguayan culture is a fusion of European and Southern Guaraní traditions: more than 80% of Paraguayans speak both Spanish and Guaraní. The ruins of two eighteenth-century Jesuit missions, La Santísima Trinidad de Paraná and Jesús de Tavarangue, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Paraguay is a founding member of Mercosur, the United Nations and the Organization of American States.
paramaribo: Paramaribo lies on the banks of the Suriname River, about 15 kilometres inland from the Atlantic Ocean, in the Paramaribo District. The city is named for the Paramaribo people who lived at the mouth of the river, and the name is from the Tupi-Guarani para, large river, and maribo, inhabitants. The name is probably a corruption of the name of a native village, spelled Parmurbo in the earliest Dutch sources. It has a tropical rainforest climate with no true dry season.

The first Dutch settlement at the site was a trading post established in 1613 by Nicolaes Baliestel and Dirck Claeszoon van Sanen. English and French traders also tried to settle in Suriname, including a French post founded in 1644 near the present city. All these early settlements were abandoned before English settlers, sent by the governor of Barbados, Lord Francis Willoughby, arrived in 1650. They founded a town on the site, protected by Fort Willoughby, and in 1662 King Charles II granted Willoughby the settlement and its surrounding lands. Around 1665 the village of Paramaribo was expanded and quickly outranked the earlier settlement of Torarica.

In 1667, during the Second Anglo-Dutch War, a squadron under Abraham Crijnssen conquered Paramaribo, and the Treaty of Breda in 1667 confirmed it as the leading town of the Dutch colony of Suriname. The fort was renamed Fort Zeelandia after the Dutch province that had financed the fleet. The population has always been diverse. Many of the first British settlers were Jews, and the Neveh Shalom Synagogue, one of the oldest synagogues in the Americas, stands in the city. The population grew greatly after 1873, when formerly enslaved people, freed in 1863, were allowed to stop working for their former masters and to leave the sugar plantations.

Fires repeatedly devastated the old town, notably in January 1821, when over 400 buildings were destroyed, and in September 1832, when nearly 50 were lost. The enslaved men Kodjo, Mentor and Present were found guilty of arson and burnt alive. Paramaribo has remained the capital of Suriname through its colonial days and the independence of 1975.

Paramaribo is the capital and largest city of Suriname and holds almost half of the country's population. The Dutch colonial town of the 17th and 18th centuries along the left bank of the river became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002, and its original architecture and street plan have largely remained intact. Landmarks include Fort Zeelandia, the Presidential Palace, the Roman Catholic cathedral of St Peter and St Paul, the Suriname Mosque and the Kwakoe memorial to the abolition of slavery. The city is the business and financial centre of the country.
paris: Paris lies in northern central France, in a north-bending arc of the river Seine, whose crest includes two islands, the Île Saint-Louis and the larger Île de la Cité, which form the oldest part of the city. The Seine's mouth on the English Channel is about 375 kilometres downstream. The city is relatively flat, with its lowest point 35 metres above sea level, and the highest of its hills, Montmartre, rises to 130 metres. Excluding the outlying parks, it covers an oval of about 87 square kilometres, enclosed by the 35-kilometre ring road, the Boulevard Périphérique, and since an annexation in 1860 it has had 20 arrondissements.

The Parisii, a Gallic tribe, inhabited the Paris area from around the middle of the 3rd century BCE. A major north–south trade route crossed the Seine on the Île de la Cité, which gradually became an important trading centre, and the Parisii traded with river towns as far away as the Iberian Peninsula and minted their own coins.

Julius Caesar conquered the Paris Basin for the Roman Republic in 52 BCE, and the Roman town of Lutetia grew on the Left Bank into a prosperous city with a forum, baths, temples, theatres and an amphitheatre. By the end of the Western Roman Empire it was known as Parisius. According to legend, Saint Denis, the first Bishop of Paris, introduced Christianity in the middle of the 3rd century CE and was beheaded on the hill later called Montmartre.

For almost all of its history, except for a few brief periods, Paris was governed directly by representatives of the king, emperor or president of France. In the 17th century the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture was established in 1648, and urbanism laws have been strictly controlled since the early 17th century. Between 1853 and 1870 Napoleon III and his Prefect of the Seine, Baron Haussmann, rebuilt the city centre, creating wide boulevards, standard facades of cream-grey Paris stone and major parks around the centre.

Paris is the capital and largest city of France, with a city population of 2.04 million and a metropolitan population of 13.3 million. The National Assembly granted it municipal autonomy in 1974, and Jacques Chirac became its first elected mayor in March 1977. Its population peaked at 2.9 million in 1921. In the 19th and early 20th centuries artists including Manet, Monet and Renoir worked there, and Impressionism, Cubism and Art Deco all evolved in the city. It hosts UNESCO, whose headquarters have been there since November 1958, and the OECD, and it has hosted the Summer Olympics in 1900, 1924 and 2024.
pataliputra: Pataliputra stood where the Ganges, the Gandhaka and the Son rivers met, a position that made it a water fort, or jaldurga, and let it dominate the river trade of the Indo-Gangetic Plain. One traditional etymology derives the name from the pāṭalī tree; another makes it the son of Pāṭali, daughter of a Raja Sudarsan. The city was also called Kusumapura, city of flowers. The Greek ambassador Megasthenes, who lived there under the Maurya Empire and called it Palibothra, described a city in the shape of a parallelogram, surrounded by a ditch and a wall with 570 towers and 64 gates. Strabo adds that the walls were of wood.

The place began as a village, Pataligrama, fortified by the Magadha ruler Ajatashatru; the date given is 490 BCE. Jain and Hindu sources name his son Udayabhadra as the king who moved the capital there from Rajgriha. Archaeological evidence shows urban growth no earlier than the 3rd or 4th century BCE. Under Ashoka it was one of the world's largest cities, with an estimated population of 150,000 to 400,000, and early Buddhist texts record the Third Buddhist council there.

Faxian, visiting about 400, found the people rich and described hospitals where the poor were treated without charge. Xuanzang in 637 found the old city in ruins, with a small walled town of about 1,000 people by the river. Suggested causes of the decline are a shift in the course of the Ganges, a flood on the Son recorded in a later Jain work and placed in the late 500s, and destruction by Hunas in the early 500s. An inscription of the Pala king Dharmapala from the early 800s describes it as a river port and royal camp. Sher Shah Suri later made it his capital under the name Patna.

Much of the ancient city lies buried under modern Patna. Its site was first identified in modern times by Laurence Waddell in 1892, and excavations have been made at Kumhrar, Bulandi Bagh and Agam Kuan. They have found stretches of the wooden palisade over several kilometres, but no stone fortifications. At Kumhrar the remains thin out from the 300s and stop about 600, and a thick layer of ash in the hall of 80 pillars suggests that it was burnt.
paul-doumer: Joseph Athanase Doumer, commonly known as Paul, was born on 22 March 1857 at Aurillac in the Cantal department into a family of modest means. A former student of the Conservatoire national des arts et métiers, he became a professor of mathematics at Mende in 1877 and taught at Remiremont from 1879 to 1883, leaving on health grounds to become chief editor of a regional newspaper, the Courrier de l'Aisne. In 1878 he married Blanche Richel. They had eight children, four of whom were killed in the First World War. He was initiated into Freemasonry in 1879 and became Grand Secretary of the Grand Orient de France in 1892.

Doumer entered politics in 1885 as chef de cabinet to Charles Floquet, president of the Chamber of Deputies, and was elected Radical deputy for the Aisne in 1888. Defeated in 1889, he was returned in 1890 by the arrondissement of Auxerre. As minister of finance in 1895–1896 he tried without success to introduce an income tax.

When he arrived in Indochina the colonies were losing millions of francs a year, and his taxes were meant to put them on a paying basis. Vietnamese, Cambodians and Laotians who could not or would not pay lost their houses and land and often became day labourers. He made Indochina a market for French products and a field for French investment. In 1898 he persuaded the French government to approve the railway to Yunnan, with a view to annexing the south of that province.

Back in France he was elected deputy for Laon, refused to support the ministry of Émile Combes and led a group of dissident Radicals that eventually helped bring it down. He was president of the Chamber from 1902 to 1905, minister of finance again in 1925 and president of the Senate from 1927. On 13 May 1931 he was elected president of the Republic, defeating the better-known Aristide Briand.

On 6 May 1932, at the opening of a book fair at the Hôtel Salomon de Rothschild in Paris, Doumer was shot by Paul Gorguloff, a Russian émigré, while talking to the author Claude Farrère. He died in hospital at 04:37 on 7 May, the second French president to be assassinated and the first to be shot. Gorguloff wrote that the act was a protest on behalf of exiled White Russians and against France's relations with the Soviet Union; he was guillotined four months later. Doumer wrote L'Indo-Chine française (1904) and Le Livre de mes fils (1906).
pennsylvania: Pennsylvania is officially the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. It lies in the Mid-Atlantic, Northeastern, Appalachian and Great Lakes regions, and is bordered by Delaware, Maryland, West Virginia, Ohio, New York, New Jersey and, across Lake Erie, the Canadian province of Ontario. The Mason-Dixon line forms its southern boundary. The Appalachian Mountains run through its centre, and about 59 per cent of the state is forested. Of the original Thirteen Colonies, it is the only one that does not border the Atlantic Ocean, though it has waterfront on Lake Erie and the tidal Delaware River.

Humans lived in what is now Pennsylvania for thousands of years before the colony was founded. The Meadowcroft Rockshelter in Jefferson Township holds the earliest known signs of human activity in the state and perhaps in all of North America, and may pre-date the Clovis culture. By 1000 CE the native population had developed agricultural techniques and a mixed food economy. Between 1638 and 1655 a south-eastern portion of the state was part of New Sweden, a Swedish colony.

In 1681 a royal land grant gave the territory to William Penn, son of the man after whom it is named. The colonial Province of Pennsylvania was known for relatively peaceful relations with native peoples, an innovative system of government and religious pluralism. Philadelphia hosted the First and Second Continental Congress; the latter formed the Continental Army under George Washington in 1775 and unanimously adopted the Declaration of Independence the following year. On 12 December 1787 Pennsylvania was the second state to ratify the United States Constitution, after Delaware. It has been known as the Keystone State since 1802, for its central place among the original colonies.

The capital is Harrisburg, and the largest cities are Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. The 2020 census counted 13,011,844 residents. The state has had five constitutions, in 1776, 1790, 1838, 1874 and 1968. Its industrial past gave it the lesser nicknames of the Coal State, the Oil State and the Steel State, and its five manufacturing centres were Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Erie, Scranton-Wilkes-Barre and the Lehigh Valley.
periodic-table: In 1817 the German physicist Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner began one of the earliest attempts to classify the elements. In 1829 he found that he could form some of them into groups of three with related properties, which he termed triads. Chlorine, bromine and iodine formed a triad, as did calcium, strontium and barium. Later chemists found more relationships between small groups of elements but could not build one scheme that took in all of them.

In 1864 John Newlands published an article in Chemical News showing that if the elements are arranged by atomic weight, every eighth element repeats the properties of the first, like the eighth note of an octave in music, which he called the Law of Octaves. The same year a book by the German chemist Lothar Meyer contained an early table of 28 elements, grouped into six families by valence, the first grouping of elements in that way.

The periodic table arranges the chemical elements in rows called periods and columns called groups, and elements in the same group tend to show similar chemical characteristics. Each element has a unique atomic number, the number of protons in its nucleus, and the elements are listed in order of increasing atomic number. A new row starts when a new electron shell has its first electron, and the columns are determined by the electron configuration of the atom. The table depicts the periodic law, which states that when elements are arranged by atomic number an approximate recurrence of their properties is evident.

Metallic character increases going down a group and from right to left across a period. The first generally accepted table was that of the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, who formulated the law as a dependence of chemical properties on atomic mass. Because not all elements were then known, his table had gaps, and he used the law to predict properties of some missing elements. The law was explained early in the 20th century by the discovery of atomic numbers and by work in quantum mechanics, and a recognisably modern form was reached in 1945 with Glenn T. Seaborg's discovery that the actinides are f-block rather than d-block elements.

The periodic law was recognised as a fundamental discovery in the late 19th century, and the table is an icon of chemistry, also widely used in physics and other sciences. In nature only elements up to atomic number 94 exist; later ones are synthetic. By 2010 the first 118 elements were known, completing the first seven rows. Within 100 years of Mendeleev's table, Edward G. Mazurs had collected an estimated 700 different published versions and there is no consensus on whether an optimal form exists.
persian-gulf: The Persian Gulf, sometimes called the Arabian Gulf, is a mediterranean sea in West Asia of some 251,000 square kilometres. It is 989 kilometres long and about 56 kilometres wide at its narrowest, in the Strait of Hormuz, which joins it to the Gulf of Oman. The water is shallow, averaging 50 metres in depth. At its north-western end the Shatt al-Arab delta carries the waters of the Euphrates and the Tigris. Eight states have coasts on it: Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

During most of the Last Glacial Period much of the Gulf was dry land, a floodplain where several rivers met. The modern sea formed as sea levels rose between about 12,000 and 6,000 years ago. Seagoing vessels from the mid-sixth millennium BCE have been found at H3 in Kuwait, when the Gulf belonged to a trade network linking Ubaid settlements in Mesopotamia with communities along its coast. At the end of the fourth millennium BCE the Dilmun civilization dominated its southern part. Between 625 BCE and 226 CE a succession of Persian empires held the northern side, and the Achaemenid navy kept bases on the Shatt al-Arab and in Bahrain, Oman and Yemen.

In 1521 a Portuguese force under Antonio Correia invaded Bahrain for its pearl industry, after Afonso de Albuquerque had captured the kingdom of Hormuz. On 29 April 1602 Shah Abbas of the Safavid Empire expelled the Portuguese from Bahrain, and in 1622, with British naval support, he took the island of Hormuz; trade moved to Bandar Abbas. Piracy was prevalent until the nineteenth century, and the British mounted the Persian Gulf campaign of 1819, which led to the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 with the sheikhs of the Pirate Coast. From 1763 until 1971 Britain held varying degrees of political control over several Gulf states.

The name Persian Gulf is the historical and internationally established one, though Arab governments use Arabian Gulf or the Gulf. The Gulf and its coastlands hold very large reserves of petroleum and natural gas, and Qatar and Iran share the largest gas field across the median line.
persian-language: Modern Persian is a continuation of Middle Persian, an official language of the Sasanian Empire (224–651 CE), which was itself a continuation of Old Persian, used in the Achaemenid Empire (550–330 BCE). It originated in the region of Fars in southwestern Iran. Old Persian is attested in cuneiform inscriptions from the 6th to the 4th century BCE, the oldest being the Behistun Inscription from the time of King Darius I (reigned 522–486 BCE). Middle Persian is attested in Pahlavi and Manichaean scripts, and New Persian literature was first recorded in the ninth century, after the Muslim conquest of Persia. Gernot Windfuhr treats New Persian as an evolution of both earlier stages, but states that none of the known Middle Persian dialects is its direct predecessor.

Persian belongs to the Western Iranian group of the Iranian languages. It has three standard varieties: Iranian Persian, Dari in Afghanistan and Tajiki in Tajikistan, all based on classic Persian literature and mutually intelligible to a relatively high degree. Iranian Persian and Dari are written in the Persian alphabet, a modified form of the Arabic alphabet; after the Arab conquest it took about 200 years before Persians adopted the Arabic script in place of Pahlavi. Tajiki is written in a Cyrillic alphabet.

Modern Persian has no grammatical gender and its usual word order is subject–object–verb. Its core vocabulary is of Middle Persian origin, but it also contains a considerable number of Arabic loanwords. John R. Perry estimates that about 20 percent of everyday vocabulary, and around 25 percent of that of classical and modern literature, is of Arabic origin.

Persian was the first language to break the monopoly of Arabic on writing in the Muslim world, and Persian poetry became a tradition in many eastern courts. It served as a language of bureaucracy even for non-native speakers, among them the Ottomans in Anatolia, the Delhi Sultanates and Mughals in the Indian subcontinent, and the Pashtuns in Afghanistan. It influenced Turkic, Armenian, Georgian, Greek and Indo-Aryan languages, as well as other Iranian ones. Works written in it include the Shahnameh by Ferdowsi, the works of Rumi, the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, the Divân of Hafez and the Gulistan and Bustan by Saadi Shirazi. Approximately 130 million people speak it worldwide.
perth: Perth lies mostly on the sandy, relatively flat Swan Coastal Plain, between the Darling Scarp and the Indian Ocean. The Swan River, also known as Derbarl Yerrigan, runs through it; the Dutch captain Willem de Vlamingh named it for the black swans he found there when exploring in 1697. The central business district and the port of Fremantle both stand on the river. Summers are hot, sunny and dry and winters mild and wet, a hot-summer Mediterranean climate. The nearest city of more than 100,000 people is Adelaide, over 2,100 km away, which makes Perth one of the most isolated major cities in the world.

People have lived in the Perth area for at least 48,000 years. Noongar country covers the south-west corner of Western Australia, and the wetlands of the Swan Coastal Plain hold spiritual importance and were a source of food. The Whadjuk Noongar are the traditional owners of the land, and the Noongar name for the place is Boorloo. In 1619 the Dutch explorer Frederick de Houtman sighted the coast near present-day Perth, which he and Jacob Dedel called Dedelsland.

Perth was founded as the administrative centre of the Swan River Colony in 1829, the first comprehensive European settlement in the west of the continent, after New South Wales had set up a convict-supported outpost at King George's Sound in 1826 in response to rumours of French annexation. Stirling's proclamation of the colony was read at Fremantle on 18 June 1829. The name honours Sir George Murray, Secretary of State for War and the Colonies, who sat in the House of Commons for Perthshire. The colony was officially designated Western Australia in 1832.

In 1850, at the request of farmers and businesspeople short of labour, Western Australia accepted convicts, and over eighteen years 9,721 arrived on 43 ships, outnumbering the roughly 7,300 free settlers. Queen Victoria announced Perth's designation as a city in 1856, but it remained a tranquil town. After a referendum in 1900 Western Australia joined the Federation of Australia in 1901, the last colony to agree, and only after concessions that included a transcontinental railway from Port Augusta to Kalgoorlie. From 1927 to 1954 Indigenous people were prohibited from entering large parts of Perth.

Perth is the capital and largest city of Western Australia and the fourth most populous city in Australia, a position it has held since 1984. Mining booms in the late 20th century made it the headquarters of significant mining operations in the state. Kings Park and Botanic Garden is one of the world's largest inner-city parks, and Fremantle Prison is a World Heritage Site.
peru: Peru covers 1,285,216 km2 on the Pacific coast of South America, the third-largest country on the continent. The Andes run parallel to the ocean and define three traditional regions: the costa, a narrow and largely arid coastal plain; the sierra, the highlands, which include the Altiplano and the highest peak, Huascarán at 6,768 metres; and the selva, the Amazon rainforest, which covers almost 60 percent of the country.

The Amazon basin covers 75% of Peruvian territory, and Lake Titicaca, shared with Bolivia, is the largest lake in South America. The name may derive from Birú, a local ruler near the Bay of San Miguel in Panama, and the Capitulation of Toledo of 1529 gave it legal status as the name of the province that was the Inca Empire.

The earliest evidence of people in Peruvian territory, about 12,500 BCE, comes from Huaca Prieta. The Caral-Supe civilization flourished on the coast, and the Chavín culture, from 1500 to 300 BCE, was probably more a religious than a political phenomenon. Later coastal cultures included the Paracas, Nazca, Moche and Chimu. The Chimu flourished from about 1140 to 1450 as a loose confederation of walled cities with its capital at Chan Chan, and in the highlands the Tiahuanaco and Wari cultures developed large urban settlements between 500 and 1000 CE.

The Spanish Empire conquered the region in the 16th century, and Charles V established a viceroyalty, the Kingdom of Peru, with its capital at Lima. According to the historian Noble David Cook, the Amerindian population fell from nearly 5–9 million in the 1520s to around 600,000 in 1620, mainly from infectious disease. The National University of San Marcos was founded in Lima in 1551. Peru proclaimed independence in 1821 and completed it in 1824, with the battle of Ayacucho. Guano exploitation brought relative stability until the War of the Pacific, 1879–1884.

Peru is a unitary semi-presidential republic under its 1993 constitution, with a president elected for five years without immediate re-election. The population was 33,396,698 in estimates to 2022, about 80 percent of them urban, and the Lima metropolitan area has over 9.8 million people. Spanish is the main language, but many Peruvians speak Quechuan languages, Aymara or other Indigenous languages.
peter-paul-rubens: Rubens was born on 28 June 1577 to Jan Rubens and Maria Pypelincks, whose family came from Antwerp. His father, a lawyer, converted to Calvinism, and in 1568 the family fled to Cologne, fearing persecution under the Duke of Alba. After Jan Rubens died in 1587 the family moved to Antwerp, where Peter Paul studied Latin and classical literature. In 1590 he had to start working, and after serving as a page to a countess he began an apprenticeship with the landscape painter Tobias Verhaecht in 1592.

In 1600 Rubens travelled to Italy, where in Venice he saw paintings by Titian, Veronese and Tintoretto. He entered the service of Duke Vincenzo I Gonzaga of Mantua, painting portraits of the ducal family and copying works in his collection, and in 1601 went on to Rome, where he studied classical sculpture and the art of Michelangelo, Raphael and Leonardo. He returned to Antwerp in 1608, and in September 1609 was appointed court painter by Archduke Albert and the Infanta Isabella Clara Eugenia, with permission to keep his studio in Antwerp. He married Isabella Brant on 3 October 1609, and from 1610 he lived and worked in a villa he designed, now the Rubenshuis Museum. His pupils and collaborators included Anthony van Dyck.

In 1621 Marie de' Medici commissioned him to paint two cycles for the Luxembourg Palace in Paris, and the one on her own life was installed in 1625. After the Twelve Years' Truce ended in 1621 the Spanish Habsburg rulers entrusted him with diplomatic missions, and between 1627 and 1630 he travelled between the courts of Spain and England to seek peace between the Spanish Netherlands and the Dutch Republic. Philip IV of Spain raised him to the nobility in 1624, Cambridge gave him an honorary degree in 1629, and Charles I of England knighted him in 1630. His output was large: Michael Jaffé's catalogue lists 1,403 works, not counting the many copies made in his workshop.

In 1630 Rubens, whose first wife Isabella had died four years earlier, married the 16-year-old Helena Fourment, who became the model for the full-figured women of many of his paintings of the 1630s. In 1635 he bought the Steen, an estate outside Antwerp, and painted landscapes there. He died on 30 May 1640 of heart failure resulting from chronic gout and was buried in Saint James' Church in Antwerp, where a family chapel was completed in 1650 with an altarpiece he painted himself. He is considered the most influential artist of the Flemish Baroque, and the terms Rubensian and Rubenesque are derived from his name.
peter-the-great: Peter was born on 9 June 1672 and grew up at the Izmaylovo Estate. When his father, Tsar Alexei, died in 1676 the throne passed to Peter's half-brother Feodor III. When Feodor died in 1682 without children, the Miloslavsky and Naryshkin families, the families of Alexei's first and second wives, disputed the succession. Ivan V was next in line but was weak-minded and blind, and the Boyar Duma, the council of nobles, chose the ten-year-old Peter, with his mother Natalya Naryshkina as regent. A hole was cut in the back of the throne so that she could whisper to the two boys, who ruled jointly until Ivan's death in 1696.

In March 1697 Peter travelled to Western Europe on an 18-month journey with a large delegation, the Grand Embassy, hoping to find allies against the Ottoman Empire; he failed to enlarge the anti-Ottoman alliance. In 1699 he moved the new year from 1 September to 1 January and had years counted from the birth of Christ. In 1700 he refused to allow a new patriarch to be elected, and the church later came under a Holy Synod controlled by a procurator.

He declared war on Sweden in the Great Northern War. The Russian army was defeated at Narva in 1700, but the Swedish king Charles XII then turned against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which gave Peter time to reorganise his army. Russia captured Nöteborg, renamed Shlisselburg, and founded Saint Petersburg on the Neva, and in 1712 Peter moved the capital there from Moscow. After his victory Russia annexed much of the eastern Baltic coast and became an empire. He created a Governing Senate in 1711 and a Table of Ranks in 1722, and brutally suppressed rebellions by the Streltsy, the Bashkirs, Astrakhan and the Bulavin Rebellion.

Peter's health was never robust. He began to suffer from problems of the bladder in the winter of 1723 and died early on 8 February 1725 at the age of 52; an autopsy found his bladder infected with gangrene. He is buried in the Saints Peter and Paul Cathedral. A story that he caught his fatal illness rescuing drowning soldiers rests on a single source and is viewed with scepticism by some historians. For Old Believers he was the Antichrist, because of the calendar changes and the poll tax, and mid-19th-century Slavophiles deplored the westernisation of Russia. The so-called Will of Peter the Great was a forgery made in Paris on Napoleon's order in 1812.
peter-tordenskjold: Peter Jansen Wessel was the tenth child of the Trondheim alderman Jan Wessel. An unruly boy, he stowed away on a ship to Copenhagen in 1704 and tried without success to become a naval cadet. The king's chaplain, Peder Jespersen, sent him on a voyage to the West Indies and at last found him a cadetship. After voyages to the East Indies he was made second lieutenant on 7 July 1711. The Norwegian admiral Waldemar Løvendal gave him the four-gun sloop Ormen and in June 1712 the 18-gun Løvendals Galej, against the advice of the Danish admiralty, which thought him unreliable.

He took part in the destruction of Swedish transports at Rügen on 29 September 1712. On 26 and 27 July 1714, off Lindesnes, he fought the 28-gun Swedish privateer Olbing Galley until both ships were badly damaged, then sent to thank her crew and to ask for more ammunition so as to go on. King Frederick IV had him court-martialled for disclosing his lack of ammunition and for risking his ship against a stronger one; he was acquitted on 15 December and made captain on 28 December.

At Kolberg on 24 April 1715 he captured the Swedish Rear-Admiral Hans Wachtmeister and the frigate Hvita Örn, which became his flagship. At Dynekilen on 8 July 1716, with two frigates and five smaller ships, he took or destroyed around 30 Swedish vessels. A failure against the Gothenburg squadron in 1717 brought a second court-martial in 1718, which was quashed after Ulrik Christian Gyldenløve intervened. He became rear-admiral in December 1718 and vice-admiral after partly destroying and partly capturing the Gothenburg squadron on 26 September 1719.

On 12 November 1720, aged 30, he was killed by the sword of the Livonian colonel Jakob Axel Staël von Holstein in a duel at Gleidingen near Hildesheim. The quarrel arose at a dinner where Tordenskiold spoke of a friend cheated at gambling. As duelling was against Danish law, his body was brought to Holmen Church without much ceremony. He is named in the Danish anthem Kong Christian stod ved højen mast of 1778 and the Norwegian anthem Ja, vi elsker dette landet of 1864. A story that at Marstrand his men moved from post to post to seem more numerous gave Danish and Norwegian the phrase Tordenskjold's soldiers.
petrarch: Petrarch was born on 20 July 1304, the son of Ser Petracco and his wife Eletta Canigiani. His birth name was Francesco di Petracco, which he Latinized to Franciscus Petrarcha. His family followed Pope Clement V to Avignon, where the papacy had moved in 1309. His father, a notary, insisted that he and his brother Gherardo study law, at Montpellier from 1316 to 1320 and at Bologna from 1320 to 1326. Petrarch preferred Latin literature and thought the seven years wasted. His father once threw his books into a fire.

After their parents died, Petrarch and his brother returned to Avignon in 1326, where he held clerical offices that left time for writing. His Latin epic Africa, about the Roman general Scipio Africanus, made him a European celebrity. On 8 April 1341 he was crowned on the Capitoline Hill in Rome by the senators Giordano Orsini and Orso dell'Anguillara, the second poet laureate since classical antiquity. He travelled widely and served as an ambassador.

He collected crumbling Latin manuscripts, and in 1345 he found in the Chapter Library of Verona Cathedral a collection of Cicero's letters not known to have survived, the Epistulae ad Atticum. About 1368 he moved with his daughter Francesca and her family to Arquà in the Euganean Hills near Padua, where he spent his remaining years in religious contemplation. The da Carrara lords of Padua seized his library, and its manuscripts are now scattered across Europe.

Petrarch is best known for the Rerum vulgarium fragmenta, or Canzoniere, a collection of 366 poems, 317 of them sonnets. The poems centre on Laura, whom he said he first saw in the church of Sainte-Claire d'Avignon on 6 April 1327. She may have been Laura de Noves, though he always denied that she was an invented figure. The Petrarchan sonnet still bears his name, and in the 16th century Pietro Bembo made his verse a model for the Italian language.

Most of his writing was in Latin, including the Secretum, an imagined dialogue with a figure inspired by Augustine of Hippo, and a large body of letters. He valued the study of ancient history and literature as the study of human thought and action, and is often called the father of humanism. He is credited with creating the idea of a historical "Dark Ages", a notion most modern scholars find inaccurate and misleading.
philadelphia: Philadelphia lies on the Atlantic Seaboard Fall Line, which separates the Atlantic Plain from the Piedmont. The Delaware and Schuylkill rivers are its principal natural bodies of water. The city encompasses about 142.7 square miles, 6 per cent of it water, and its highest point, in Chestnut Hill, is about 446 feet above sea level. The city has been coterminous with its county since 1854.

Before Europeans arrived in the early 17th century, the Lenape, also known as the Delaware Indians, lived in the village of Shackamaxon, in present-day Philadelphia. Most Lenape were pushed out of the region during the 18th century as the Thirteen Colonies expanded, a loss made worse by intertribal conflicts, newly introduced diseases, mainly smallpox, and conflicts with Europeans. In the 1860s the federal government sent most of those remaining in the eastern United States to the Indian Territory, in present-day Oklahoma.

William Penn, an English Quaker and advocate of religious freedom, founded Philadelphia in 1682, and it became the capital of the colonial Province of Pennsylvania. It hosted the First Continental Congress in 1774 and the Second Continental Congress, which formed the Continental Army, elected George Washington as its commander and adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776. The British Army occupied the city for nine months, from September 1777 to June 1778. The Constitution of the United States was ratified at the Philadelphia Convention. The city served as the national capital on several occasions until 1800, when the new capital at Washington, D.C. was completed.

Philadelphia is the most populous city in Pennsylvania and the sixth most populous in the United States, with about 1.6 million people in the 2020 census. Independence National Historical Park, which holds Independence Hall and the Liberty Bell, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the city has 67 National Historic Landmarks. It claims many firsts in the United States, among them the first library (1731), hospital (1751), medical school (1765) and zoo (1874).
philippines: The Philippines consists of about 7,641 islands with a total area of about 300,000 km2, stretching 1,850 kilometres from north to south. They fall into three divisions, Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao, and the 11 largest islands make up about 95 percent of the land. The highest mountain is Mount Apo on Mindanao, at 2,954 metres.

The islands lie on the western fringes of the Pacific Ring of Fire, with 23 active volcanoes and about five recorded earthquakes a day, most too weak to be felt. On an expedition of the 16th century Ruy López de Villalobos named Leyte and Samar Felipinas after the Prince of Asturias, later Philip II of Castile, and the name Las Islas Filipinas was later used for the Spanish possessions. The title Republic of the Philippines appeared in the 1935 constitution.

Evidence of early hominins dates to as early as 709,000 years ago, and bones from Callao Cave may represent an unknown species, Homo luzonensis, who lived 50,000 to 67,000 years ago. The first Austronesians reached the islands from Taiwan around 2200 BCE and settled the Batanes Islands and northern Luzon. The earliest known surviving written record is the Laguna Copperplate Inscription of 900 CE, in Old Malay. By the 14th century large coastal settlements had become trading centres, trade with China had begun under the late Tang dynasty and widened under the Song, and Islam was established in the Sulu Archipelago by the 15th century.

Ferdinand Magellan's arrival marked the beginning of Spanish colonization. Catholicism became the dominant religion, and Manila became the western hub of trans-Pacific trade. The Philippine Revolution began in 1896 and became entwined with the Spanish–American War of 1898, after which Spain ceded the territory to the United States and revolutionaries declared the First Philippine Republic. The ensuing Philippine–American War left the United States in control until the Japanese invasion in the Second World War, and the Philippines became independent in 1946.

Ferdinand Marcos ruled under martial law from 1972 to 1981, and the People Power Revolution overthrew him in 1986. The Philippines is a constitutional republic with a presidential system, in which the president serves a six-year term, and its population was 112,729,484 in July 2024. The largest ethnic group in the 2020 census was the Tagalog, at 26.0 percent, and indigenous peoples comprise 110 ethnolinguistic groups. Spanish and American rule left lasting marks, among them the dominance of Catholicism, the use of English and Spanish surnames resulting from an 1849 edict.
phnom-penh: Phnom Penh lies in the south-central region of Cambodia, on the banks of the Tonlé Sap, the Mekong and the Bassac rivers, and is fully surrounded by Kandal province. It is a typical flood plain, and flooding in the monsoon season is a problem when the river sometimes overflows its banks. The city takes its name from Wat Phnom, the hill temple, and from Lady Penh, its founder.

Excavations at Choeung Ek, in the south of the city, uncovered one of the largest kiln pottery centres in Cambodia, which produced ceremonial vessels from the 5th to the 13th century, and suggest settlement from the 5th century. According to a tale first recorded a century after it is said to have taken place, a woman named Penh found a floating koki tree in the river in 1372. Inside it were four Buddha statues and one of Vishnu, and she raised a hill with a shrine to house them, later known as Wat Phnom.

King Ponhea Yat moved the capital here from Angkor Thom after Siam captured and destroyed it. Later kings abandoned Phnom Penh because of fighting between royal pretenders and set up their capitals at places such as Pursat, Longvek and Oudong. Japanese immigrants settled on the outskirts of the city in the 17th century, and a Portuguese community carried on commercial and religious activity there. It became the capital again in 1865 and was the national capital under French colonial rule. After independence it was modernized, and earned the nickname the Pearl of Asia for its French colonial, New Khmer and Art Deco architecture.

During the Vietnam War thousands of refugees fled to the city from the fighting, and by 1975 its population was two to three million. The Khmer Rouge cut off supplies for more than a year before the city fell on 17 April 1975, and then forcibly evacuated all its residents. The city faced persecution, forced labour and genocide, and remained largely uninhabited until Vietnam-backed forces took it in 1979, when people began to return. Reconstruction followed with foreign investment and aid.

Phnom Penh is the capital and most populous city of Cambodia and the seat of its monarchy at the Royal Palace. It is an autonomous municipality with a status equal to that of the provinces. The official language is Khmer, and English and French are also used. Its census population was 2,129,371 in 2019. Its Water Festival marks the reversing of the flow of the Tonlé Sap River, and the city holds buildings of the New Khmer Architecture of the 1950s and 1960s, associated with the architect Vann Molyvann.
plato: Plato was born in the late fifth century BCE into an aristocratic and influential Athenian family. Through his mother, Perictione, he was a descendant of Solon, the statesman credited with laying the foundations of Athenian democracy. Diogenes Laertius asserted that Plato was a nickname alluding to his robust figure and that his birth name was Aristocles, but modern scholarship widely regards this as false. His brothers Glaucon and Adeimantus appear in the Republic. During his childhood Athens was at war with Sparta in the Peloponnesian War, and both brothers distinguished themselves at the battle of Megara in 409 BCE.

Like all male citizens of Athens, Plato received a traditional education in gymnastics and music. Ancient writers report a tradition that in his youth he wrote poems and tragedies, but burnt them when he met Socrates and turned to philosophy. He soon became a member of Socrates' inner circle. Socrates examined the ideas of his interlocutors by a series of questions, the Socratic method, and turned philosophy from natural philosophy to questions of ethics and politics.

Plato wrote dialogues in which Socrates is usually the primary speaker. Plato never presents himself as a participant. The dialogues discuss religion, human nature, love, perception and reality, and body and soul. His best known contribution is the theory of Forms, first introduced in the Phaedo. It holds that there is an apparent world of material objects grasped by the senses, which constantly changes, and an unchanging and unseen world of Forms, grasped by reason. He also argued for the immortality of the soul, and in the Republic the soul has three parts.

Thirty-five dialogues and thirteen letters have traditionally been ascribed to Plato, though modern scholarship doubts the authenticity of at least some of them. No one knows the exact order in which the dialogues were written. During the Islamic Golden Age, Neoplatonism was revived, and Al-Farabi, inspired by the Republic, proposed an ideal city governed by philosopher-kings. Byzantine scholars reintroduced Plato's texts to Western Europe in the early Renaissance, and about 250 Byzantine manuscripts survive. The edition published by Henricus Stephanus in Geneva in 1578 established the standard Stephanus pagination still in use.
plutarch: Plutarch was born to a prominent family in the small town of Chaeronea, in the Greek region of Boeotia, about 30 kilometres east of Delphi. His family was long established there. His father was named Autobulus and his grandfather Lamprias, and his brothers Timon and Lamprias appear often in his essays and dialogues. He studied mathematics and philosophy in Athens under Ammonius from 66 to 67 CE. At some point he received Roman citizenship, sponsored by Lucius Mestrius Florus, an associate of the emperor Vespasian, and took the name Lucius Mestrius Plutarchus.

Plutarch lived most of his life at Chaeronea, where he served as a magistrate and held the office of archon,. He visited Rome about 70 CE with Florus, who served as a source for his Life of Otho, and he was on familiar terms with Roman nobles including Quintus Sosius Senecio. About 95 CE he became one of the two priests of the temple of Apollo at Delphi, a site that had declined considerably since the classical period. He was also epimeletes of the Amphictyonic League for at least five terms, from 107 to 127, organising the Pythian Games. Plutarch and his wife Timoxena had at least four sons and one daughter. The year of his death is not known.

His best-known work, the Parallel Lives, arranges biographies of illustrious Greeks and Romans in pairs to illuminate their shared virtues and vices. The surviving Lives contain 23 pairs and four single lives, though several others are lost and many survivors are truncated. Plutarch states in his Life of Alexander that he is writing lives and not histories, because a small thing such as a phrase or a jest often reveals character better than battles. His Life of Pyrrhus is the main account of Roman history from 293 to 264 BCE, for which the texts of Dionysius and Livy are lost.

The Moralia is a collection of seventy-eight essays and speeches. It includes a dialogue on the face seen in the orb of the Moon, which served as a source for Galileo, On the Worship of Isis and Osiris, a crucial source on ancient Egyptian religion, and philosophical treatises such as On the Decline of the Oracles. Some works printed with it, including the Lives of the Ten Orators, were falsely attributed to him and are credited to an unknown author called Pseudo-Plutarch.
podgorica: Podgorica lies in central Montenegro, at the confluence of the Ribnica and Morača rivers, where the southern foothills of the Dinaric Alps meet the northernmost part of the Zeta Plain. The name means under the hill. The city is only 15 kilometres north of Lake Skadar and stands at the crossroads of several historically important routes, in fertile lowlands with a favourable climate.

The oldest physical remains in the area are from the late Stone Age. In the Iron Age the area between the Zeta and Bjelopavlići valleys was populated by two Illyrian tribes, the Labeates and the Docleatae, and the nearby town of Doclea had 8,000 to 10,000 inhabitants. The area later passed through many hands, among them the Roman Empire, the Byzantine Empire, the Serbian Empire and the Republic of Venice.

The Ottoman Empire captured Podgorica in 1474, and in 1479 built a large fortress there. The existing settlement, with its highly developed merchant connections, became the main Ottoman defensive and attacking bastion in the region. After the Congress of Berlin in 1878 the town was annexed to the Principality of Montenegro, ending four centuries of Ottoman rule. Roads were built to all neighbouring towns in 1902, and tobacco became its first significant commercial product.

In World War II Podgorica was bombed over 80 times, first by the Luftwaffe on 6 April 1941; an attack by the USAAF on 5 May 1944 killed about 400 civilians. It was liberated on 19 December 1944, and 1,691 people had been killed there in the course of the war. Josip Broz Tito promised on 12 July 1946 that the destroyed city would be rebuilt. It was renamed Titograd in 1946 and designated capital of the Socialist Republic of Montenegro, and rapid growth turned a small town into the country's primate city. Its original name was restored after a referendum on 2 April 1992.

Podgorica is the capital and largest city of Montenegro, capital of the independent state since 2006. It is a hub of the country's rail and road network and the centre of its education, science and healthcare. Cetinje, capital for much of Montenegrin history, preserves much of the national cultural heritage. Monuments in and around Podgorica include the Clock tower, the ruins of the Ribnica fortress and remnants of the ancient city of Doclea.
poland: Poland covers an administrative area of 312,722 square kilometres, the ninth-largest country in Europe. The central and northern parts bordering the Baltic Sea lie within the flat Central European Plain, while the south is hilly and mountainous. The Sudetes lie in the west and the Carpathians in the east, and the Tatra Mountains hold the highest point, the northwestern summit of Rysy at 2,500 metres. The coastline spans 770 kilometres. The longest rivers are the Vistula, the Oder, the Warta and the Bug, and the country has around ten thousand lakes, mostly in the north-eastern region of Masuria.

The first Stone Age archaic humans settled the area approximately 500,000 years ago. The earliest evidence of European cheesemaking, from 5500 BCE, was discovered in Kuyavia, and a fortified settlement at Biskupin is attributed to the Lusatian culture of the Late Bronze Age. In antiquity many peoples lived in the territory, among them Celtic, Scythian, Germanic, Sarmatian, Baltic and Slavic tribes. Poland began to form into a unitary and territorial entity around the middle of the 10th century under the Piast dynasty, and in 966 the ruler of the Polans, Mieszko I, accepted Western Christianity under the Roman Catholic Church. The Kingdom of Poland emerged in 1025.

In 1569 Poland cemented its long-standing association with Lithuania, forming the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which had an elective monarchy and adopted Europe's first modern constitution in 1791. The country was partitioned by neighbouring states at the end of the 18th century and regained independence in 1918 as the Second Polish Republic.

The invasion of Poland by Germany and by the Soviet Union in September 1939 marked the beginning of World War II, which resulted in the Holocaust and millions of Polish casualties. Forced into the Eastern Bloc, the Polish People's Republic was a signatory of the Warsaw Pact. The Solidarity movement emerged in 1980, and in 1989 Poland re-established itself as a liberal democracy and held free elections.

Poland has over 37 million people and is composed of sixteen voivodeships, with Warsaw as its capital and largest city. It is a unitary parliamentary republic with a bicameral legislature of the Sejm, with 460 members, and the Senate, with 100. The 2021 census found that ethnic Poles comprise 98.84% of the population. It keeps its own currency, the złoty. Poland has 18 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
pope-francis: Jorge Mario Bergoglio was born on 17 December 1936 in Flores, a neighbourhood of Buenos Aires, the eldest of five children. His father, Mario José Bergoglio, was an accountant and an Italian immigrant from Piedmont; his mother, Regina María Sívori, was a housewife born in Buenos Aires to a family of northern Italian origin. The family left Italy in 1929 to escape the fascist rule of Benito Mussolini. At 21, after life-threatening pneumonia and three cysts, he had part of a lung removed.

Bergoglio entered the Society of Jesus as a novice on 11 March 1958, after three years at the archdiocesan seminary in Villa Devoto, and studied the humanities in Santiago, Chile. He took perpetual vows on 12 March 1960 and taught literature and psychology in Santa Fe and Buenos Aires. He was ordained in 1969 and was Jesuit provincial superior in Argentina from 1973 to 1979. In 1976 the Argentine Navy kidnapped two Jesuit priests, Orlando Yorio and Franz Jalics, during the Dirty War. Bergoglio is widely reported to have failed to protect them; a criminal complaint filed in 2005 was dismissed, but the debate over his conduct has continued.

He became archbishop of Buenos Aires on the death of his predecessor, Quarracino, on 28 February 1998, and was created a cardinal in 2001 by Pope John Paul II. He doubled the number of priests working in the city's shantytowns, which earned him the name villero bishop, and put the archdiocese's finances on a stricter footing. After the resignation of Pope Benedict XVI, the conclave elected him pope on 13 March 2013. He took the name Francis in honour of Francis of Assisi, and was the first Jesuit pope, the first from Latin America and the first from the Southern Hemisphere.
