As pope Francis called for decentralised, synodal governance, made women full members of dicasteries of the Roman Curia and convened the Synod on Synodality. He was a behind-the-scenes broker, with the Government of Canada, of the restoration of diplomatic relations between the United States and Cuba announced on 17 December 2014.

His last public appearance was on Easter Sunday, 20 April 2025. He died on Easter Monday, 21 April 2025, aged 88, of a cerebral stroke. His funeral took place on 26 April, and on 8 May the conclave elected Robert Francis Prevost as Pope Leo XIV. Francis had appointed more than 80 per cent of the cardinals who elected his successor, and he formalised the Church's opposition to the death penalty in all cases.
pope-john-paul-ii: Karol Józef Wojtyła was the youngest of three children of Karol Wojtyła, an ethnic Pole, and Emilia Kaczorowska, a schoolteacher. His mother died in 1929, when he was eight. In his youth he worked occasionally as a stage actor, and during the Second World War he took work in a quarry to avoid being sent to a German forced labour camp. Adam Stefan Sapieha, the Archbishop of Kraków, encouraged him to study theology and ordained him on 1 November 1946. On 4 July 1958 Pope Pius XII appointed him auxiliary bishop of Kraków, and at 38 he became the youngest bishop in Poland.

After Pope John Paul I died following only 33 days as pope, a second conclave opened on 14 October 1978, split between Cardinal Giuseppe Siri and Cardinal Giovanni Benelli. Cardinal Franz König suggested Wojtyła as a compromise, and he won on the eighth ballot on 16 October, taking his predecessor's name. He wrote 14 encyclicals, completed a reform of the Church's legal system and the Roman Curia, and saw the 1983 Code of Canon Law and the Catechism of the Catholic Church promulgated. He beatified 1,344 people and canonised 483 saints.

On 13 May 1981 he was shot in the abdomen in St. Peter's Square by Mehmet Ali Ağca, lost nearly three-quarters of his blood and underwent five hours of surgery. As pope he made public apologies for more than 100 wrongdoings, among them the trial of Galileo Galilei (31 October 1992) and the silence of many Catholics during the Holocaust (1998).

He died on 2 April 2005 and was succeeded by Pope Benedict XVI. He was beatified on 1 May 2011 and canonised on 27 April 2014 by Pope Francis, alongside Pope John XXIII. He has been credited with helping to end communist rule in Poland and the rest of Europe, and under him the Church greatly expanded its influence in Africa and Latin America. He has also been criticised for allegedly not acting against, or being insufficiently harsh with, the sexual abuse of children by priests, both as archbishop in the Polish People's Republic and as pope.
portuguese-language: Portuguese belongs to the Ibero-Romance group, which evolved from several dialects of Vulgar Latin in the medieval Kingdom of Galicia and the County of Portugal. Before the Roman conquest the territory of modern Portugal was inhabited by the Gallaeci, Lusitanians, Celts, Iberians, Phoenicians, Greeks and Ligurians, whose languages were gradually replaced but left words behind, many of them about nature, agriculture and material culture. The Roman presence began in 218 BCE and full consolidation came in 19 BCE under Augustus. Latin spread outward from the cities and was tied to Roman citizenship. In the 5th century the Suebi and Visigoths conquered the peninsula and contributed about 500 Germanic words, many to do with warfare.

Portuguese has a rich system of nasal vowels, and its spelling is largely phonemic but shaped by etymology and tradition. Its verbs have kept more inflections from classical Latin than any other major Romance language, and it has features that other Romance languages, except Galician and Fala, lack, among them the future subjunctive and the personal infinitive. Its lexicon of around 228,500 entries comes largely from Latin, with more than 3,000 words traced to pre-Roman Celtic sources and loanwords from Germanic, Arabic, African, Amerindian and Asian languages. It is fully mutually intelligible with Galician, with which it shares its origin in the medieval language Galician-Portuguese. Two standard varieties are used for learning, European and Brazilian Portuguese.

Colonial expansion carried Portuguese across the world. It is the official language of eight countries: Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe and Timor-Leste, and shares official status in Macau and Equatorial Guinea. There are about 267 million speakers in all, some 200 million of them in South America and 30 million in Africa. In Cape Verde and Guinea-Bissau a Portuguese-based creole is also widely spoken. The Community of Portuguese Language Countries unites all the officially Lusophone nations, and recent spelling agreements have tried to give the language one spelling everywhere.
potato: The potato is the underground stem tuber of Solanum tuberosum, a perennial in the nightshade family. Its tubers are not roots but stems that form from thickened rhizomes at the tips of long thin stolons. Wild potato species occur from the southern United States to southern Chile. Genetic studies show that the cultivated potato has a single origin, in the area of present-day southern Peru and extreme northwestern Bolivia, around Lake Titicaca, where pre-Columbian farmers domesticated it about 7,000 to 10,000 years ago from a species in the Solanum brevicaule complex.

The earliest archaeologically verified tuber remains come from the coastal site of Ancon in central Peru and date to 2500 BCE. The most widely cultivated variety, Solanum tuberosum tuberosum, is indigenous to the Chiloé Archipelago and has been grown by the local indigenous people since before the Spanish conquest.

The English word potato comes from the Spanish patata, in turn from the Taíno batata, which meant sweet potato and not the plant now called simply the potato. The name spud comes from spudde, a short and stout knife or dagger in the 15th century, and was transferred to the tuber from around 1840.

The Spanish introduced potatoes to Europe in the second half of the 16th century. Selective breeding has since produced over 5,000 varieties, about 3,000 of them in the Andes, mainly in Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Chile and Colombia. Over 100 cultivars might be found in a single valley, and a dozen or more might be maintained by a single agricultural household. Most potatoes are self-incompatible and bear no useful fruit when self-pollinated, which makes crop breeding difficult, since all sexually produced plants must be hybrids.

The potato has been an essential crop in the Andes since the pre-Columbian era. The Moche culture of northern Peru represented it in ceramics, both naturally and as human figures. In Inca mythology Axomamma, a daughter of the earth mother Pachamama, is the goddess of potatoes, who ensured the fertility of the soil and the growth of the tubers. In Haudenosaunee mythology the first potatoes grew out of the feet of Earth Woman after she died giving birth to her twin sons, Sapling and Flint. Chuño, a freeze-dried potato product, is traditionally made by Quechua and Aymara communities of Peru and Bolivia.

In Europe the potato became an essential crop, especially in Northern and Eastern Europe. In the late 19th century numerous images of potato harvesting appeared in European art, including the works of Willem Witsen and Anton Mauve. Raw potatoes contain toxic glycoalkaloids, chiefly solanine and chaconine, and tubers exposed to light can become toxic.
prague: Prague is situated on the Vltava River, into which the Berounka flows in the suburb of Lahovice. Most of the city lies on the Prague Plateau. Its highest point is the hill Teleček on the western border, at 399 metres, and its lowest is the Vltava at Suchdol, at 172 metres. The city grew from a settlement stretching from Prague Castle in the north to the fort of Vyšehrad in the south. Its archaeological deposits are over 10 metres deep. The name Praha has been explained in several ways, among them as meaning a threshold, a ford or rapid, or a burned forest cleared for settlement.

The region was settled as early as the Paleolithic. Around the fifth and fourth centuries BCE a Celtic tribe, the Boii, appeared there and gave Bohemia its name, meaning home of the Boii. They built the largest Celtic oppidum in Bohemia, at Závist, and in the last century BCE Germanic tribes slowly drove them out. The 2nd-century map of Ptolemaios mentions a Germanic city called Casurgis near the site of present-day Prague.

Prague became the capital of the Kingdom of Bohemia and the residence of several Holy Roman Emperors, most notably Charles IV, who reigned from 1346 to 1378, and Rudolf II, who reigned from 1575 to 1611. Charles University, founded in 1348, is the oldest university in Central Europe. The city played major roles in the Bohemian and Protestant Reformations and in the Thirty Years' War. It was an important city to the Habsburg monarchy and to Austria-Hungary, and the capital of Czechoslovakia in the interwar period and in the Communist era after World War II.

Prague suffered considerably less damage in World War II than some other major cities in the region, which allowed most of its historic architecture to stay true to form. The city contains buildings in many styles, from Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque to Art Nouveau and Cubist. The Estates Theatre was the venue of the premieres of Mozart's Don Giovanni and La clemenza di Tito.

Prague is the capital and largest city of the Czech Republic and the historical capital of Bohemia, with a population of about 1.4 million. It has had the status of a statutory city again since 24 November 1990. The historic centre has been on the UNESCO list of World Heritage Sites since 1992. Among its landmarks are Prague Castle, Charles Bridge, the Old Town Square with the astronomical clock, the Jewish Quarter and Vyšehrad. It has been nicknamed the City of a Hundred Spires.
pretoria: Pretoria stands about 56 kilometres north-northeast of Johannesburg, at an altitude of about 1,339 metres. It lies in a warm, sheltered, fertile valley in the transitional belt between the plateau of the Highveld to the south and the lower-lying Bushveld to the north, surrounded by the hills of the Magaliesberg range, and straddles the Apies River. It is called the Jacaranda City for the roughly 60,000 to 70,000 jacaranda trees along its streets.

Pretoria was founded in 1855 by Marthinus Pretorius, a leader of the Voortrekkers, who named it after his father Andries Pretorius and chose a spot on the banks of the Apies as the new capital of the South African Republic. The elder Pretorius had become a national hero of the Voortrekkers after his victory over Dingane and the Zulus in the Battle of Blood River in 1838, and had negotiated the Sand River Convention of 1852, in which the United Kingdom acknowledged the independence of the Transvaal. Pretoria became the capital of the republic on 1 May 1860, superseding Potchefstroom.

In the First Boer War, Republican forces besieged the city in December 1880 and March 1881, and the peace treaty was signed in Pretoria on 3 August 1881 at the Pretoria Convention. In the Second Boer War the city surrendered to British forces under Frederick Roberts on 5 June 1900, and the conflict ended in Pretoria with the Peace of Vereeniging, signed on 31 May 1902 at Melrose House. That war ended the Transvaal Republic and began British hegemony in South Africa.

In 1910 the Boer republics of the South African Republic and the Orange River Colony were united with the Cape Colony and Natal Colony as the Union of South Africa. Pretoria became the administrative capital of the whole country, with Cape Town as the legislative capital and Bloemfontein as the judicial capital, and from 1910 to 1994 it was also the capital of the province of Transvaal. It achieved official city status on 14 October 1931 and remained the administrative capital when South Africa became a republic in 1961.

Pretoria is the executive capital of South Africa, seat of the executive branch and home to all foreign embassies. It forms the central part of the City of Tshwane Metropolitan Municipality. It is an academic and research centre, with the University of Pretoria, the University of South Africa and the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research. The Voortrekker Monument and Kruger House, residence of the president of the South African Republic, are among its museums and monuments.
prince-vijaya: The Mahavamsa gives Vijaya a marvellous ancestry. His grandmother Suppadevi, daughter of the king of Vanga and a princess of Kalinga, was carried off by Sinha, the lion, whom some modern interpreters take to have been an outlaw living in the forest. Their son Sinhabahu escaped with his mother and sister, killed his father, founded the city of Sinhapura in the Lala country and married his sister Sinhasivali. Vijaya was the eldest of their thirty-two sons. Where Sinhapura lay is uncertain: it has been placed in Bengal, Odisha, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, among other places.

Made prince regent by his father, Vijaya became notorious with his followers for violent deeds, and prominent citizens demanded his death. Sinhabahu instead expelled them: their heads were half shaved and they were put on a ship, their wives and children being sent off on separate ships.

In the Mahavamsa's telling the kingdom was named Tambapanni, copper-red hands, because the red soil coloured the hands of Vijaya's men, and his people were called Sinhala after Sinhabahu. His ministers founded villages, among them Upatissagama. To be crowned he needed a queen of noble house, and the Pandya king of Madhura, identified with Madurai, sent his daughter with a hundred noble maidens, craftsmen and a thousand families of eighteen guilds, who landed at the port of Mahatittha.

Vijaya then sent Kuveni away, since his people feared supernatural beings. She went with their two children, Jivahatta and Disala, to the Yakkha city of Lankapura, where she was killed as a traitor. The children fled to Sumanakuta, and from them the chronicle derives the Pulinda, identified with the Vedda people. Vijaya, crowned, is said to have given up his evil ways and ruled in peace and justice.

Having no heir, Vijaya in old age sent for his twin brother Sumitta, but died before a reply came. His ministers governed for a year until Panduvasudeva, Sumitta's youngest son, arrived from Sinhapura to rule. The older Dipavamsa tells a similar story without Kuveni or the South Indian princess, and two other versions of the legend, one recorded by Xuanzang and one a Jataka painted at Ajanta, give the founding prince other names.

There is no archaeological evidence for the story. In Sri Lanka it is often treated as history and used in political argument: Sinhalese scholars such as K. M. de Silva have cited it for the Indo-Aryan origins of the Sinhalese, while Tamil authors such as Satchi Ponnambalam have dismissed it as fiction serving Sinhalese territorial claims.
protestantism: Protestantism follows the theology of the Protestant Reformation, a movement that began in the 16th century with the aim of reforming the Catholic Church of perceived errors and abuses. It began in the Holy Roman Empire in 1517, when Martin Luther published his Ninety-five Theses in reaction to abuses in the sale of indulgences. Luther argued against buying or earning forgiveness and claimed instead that salvation is a gift God gives to those who have faith.

The name comes from a protest. Six princes of the Holy Roman Empire and the rulers of fourteen Imperial Free Cities issued a protest against the edict of the Diet of Speyer in 1529 and were the first to be called Protestants. Lutheranism spread into Denmark–Norway, Sweden, Finland, Livonia and Iceland, and Calvinist churches spread in Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands, Scotland, Switzerland, France, Poland and Lithuania. The separation of the Church of England from the Catholic Church under King Henry VIII began Anglicanism.

Protestants hold to justification by faith alone, the priesthood of all believers, and the Bible as the highest authority for faith and practice. They reject papal supremacy, and early Protestants rejected transubstantiation. Lutherans affirmed a corporeal presence of Christ in Holy Communion, along with Catholics, while the Reformed affirmed a real spiritual presence.

The movement soon divided into branches: Lutheranism, Anglicanism, Calvinism or Reformed Christianity, and later Methodism, which grew from a revival within the 18th-century Church of England under John Wesley, and the Baptists, who hold that baptism should be given only to professing believers. The Radical Reformation, which had no state sponsorship and faced intense persecution from both Catholics and mainstream Protestants, gave rise to Anabaptism, whose descendants include the Amish, Hutterites and Mennonites.

The Reformation affected marriage and family, education, the political and social order, the economy and the arts. Protestant churches reject a celibate priesthood and allow their clergy to marry. Freedom of conscience gained priority after Luther refused to recant at the Diet of Worms in 1521, and Rhode Island, Connecticut and Pennsylvania combined democratic constitutions with freedom of religion. Protestants founded hospitals, schools and aid organisations, and in the 19th century many took part in the abolition of slavery, prison reform and woman suffrage. Estimates of the number of Protestants worldwide range from 600 million to 1 billion, because scholars disagree on which denominations count.
puerto-rico: Puerto Rico consists of a main island and smaller islands, including Vieques, Culebra and Mona. It lies about 1,000 miles south-east of Miami, between the Dominican Republic and the U.S. Virgin Islands, and is the smallest of the Greater Antilles. The Cordillera Central crosses the island from east to west. Puerto Rico is Spanish for rich port. Columbus named the island San Juan Bautista and the capital Ciudad de Puerto Rico, but traders came to call the whole island Puerto Rico, and San Juan became the name of the port and capital.

The island's history began with the Ortoiroid culture, an Archaic hunter-gatherer population present as early as about 4,000 years ago. Around 500–200 BCE Saladoid peoples from the Orinoco River basin migrated there, bringing sedentary agriculture and ceramics, and their ancestry became predominant in the populations that developed into the Taíno. The Taíno were the dominant Indigenous people when Columbus arrived in 1493. Their numbers fell sharply in the 16th century through introduced infectious diseases, exploitation by Spanish settlers and warfare.

Spain claimed the island after Columbus's arrival and Juan Ponce de León colonised it in 1508. It was a major military post in the wars between Spain and other European powers in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, and in 1593 Portuguese soldiers formed the first garrison of the San Felipe del Morro fortress. Spanish settlers, mainly from the Canary Islands and Andalusia, and African slaves changed the cultural and demographic landscape. By the late 19th century a distinct Puerto Rican identity, combining European, African and Indigenous elements, had begun to emerge.

In the 19th century Puerto Rico and Cuba were Spain's last two colonies in the New World. The Crown revived the Royal Decree of Graces of 1815, offering free land to those who swore loyalty to the Crown and the Catholic Church, in the hope that independence movements would lose strength. The United States acquired Puerto Rico in 1898 after the Spanish–American War. Puerto Ricans have been U.S. citizens since 1917, and Congress approved a territorial constitution in 1952.

Puerto Rico is officially the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, an unincorporated territory of the United States, and its political status is a continuing subject of debate. San Juan is the capital. Spanish and English are the official languages, though Spanish predominates. Old San Juan has the Cathedral of San Juan Bautista, which holds the tomb of Juan Ponce de León.
punctation-of-olmutz: The German Confederation, dominated by Austria, had been dissolved in the Revolutions of 1848 and partially succeeded by the Frankfurt Assembly. After the assembly failed, Prussia took the initiative in early 1850 with the Erfurt Union, a federation of most of the German states under its own lead. The two powers were thus in conflict over the leadership of Germany.

A dispute between the Elector of Hesse and his subjects gave the Austrian chancellor Felix zu Schwarzenberg the occasion to isolate Prussia further. Austrian and allied armies advanced into the Electorate of Hesse, and on 8 November 1850 the Prussian army came close to war with Bavaria, an ally of Austria, near Fulda-Bronnzell. In the Warsaw negotiations of October 1850 Tsar Nicholas I of Russia had already taken Austria's side, which was part of the reason why Prussia decided to give in.

The agreement, also called the Agreement of Olmütz, came out of a conference held in the town, now Olomouc in the Czech Republic, and closed the Autumn Crisis of 1850. Prussia gave up its claim to lead the German states and submitted to Austrian leadership of the restored confederation. It agreed to demobilise, to take part in the intervention of the German Diet in Hesse and in Holstein, and renounced any resumption of the Erfurt Union. Austria for its part agreed to call a conference of ministers to discuss a reform of the confederation.

The ministerial conference that Austria had promised met in Dresden the following year and ended without result, so that the confederation continued unreformed under Austrian leadership. The name of humiliation was given to the treaty because many saw in it a capitulation of the Prussians to the Austrians.
purandar-singha: Purandar Singha was born in 1807 at Silmari in British-ruled Bengal, a great-great-grandson of the Ahom king Rajeswar Singha. His grandfather and his father Brajanath Gohain had conspired against reigning kings and lived there as exiled princes in poverty. In 1818 Ruchinath Burhagohain, who held King Chandrakanta Singha responsible for bringing in the Burmese, invited Brajanath to claim the throne, and their force entered the capital Jorhat on 17 February 1818. Brajanath had coins struck in his own name, but the mutilation of one of his ears barred him from kingship, since an Ahom king had to be without blemish. His son, then ten years old, was acclaimed instead.

Real authority lay with Brajanath and Ruchinath, who removed the officers suspected of loyalty to Chandrakanta. A Burmese army of 30,000 sent by King Bodawpaya defeated the Assamese on 17 February 1819; Purandar, his father and Ruchinath fled to Guwahati with the valuables of the royal treasury, worth 3.5 million rupees. After a second defeat on 11 June 1819 they escaped to Bengal. The Governor-General Lord Hastings refused to help. They recruited soldiers in Goalpara, Bengal and Bhutan, armed with the aid of a British trader, Robert Bruce, and fought both Chandrakanta and the Burmese before withdrawing in 1822.

After the Treaty of Yandabo of 24 February 1826 the British held the Brahmaputra valley. Sensing discontent, they considered in 1832 restoring Upper Assam as a tributary princedom and chose Purandar over Chandrakanta; some historians think they expected a long-exiled prince to be the more grateful and submissive. From April 1833 he ruled from Jorhat, without Sadiya and Matak, for a tribute of 50,000 rupees. Within three years he fell behind in his payments and asked for a reduction. An enquiry by Captain Francis Jenkins found corruption and oppression, and the king himself amassing a personal fortune.

The kingdom was placed under direct British control in September 1838. Purandar stayed in Jorhat and refused the pension of 1,000 rupees a month granted in October 1838, hoping that a petition to the Governor-General would restore his state; it was turned down. When officials and adventurers dug into the royal tombs, the maidams, at Charaideo in search of treasure, he first protested and then opened many tombs himself. He died on 1 October 1846 and was entombed at Jorhat, at the place now called Raja Maidam.
pyongyang: Pyongyang lies in the west-central part of North Korea on a flat plain, about 50 kilometres east of Korea Bay, an arm of the Yellow Sea. The Taedong River flows southwestward through the city, about 109 kilometres upstream from its mouth. The Pyongyang plain is one of the two large plains on the western coast of the Korean peninsula, the other being the Chaeryong plain, each of about 500 square kilometres.

The name comes from the Sino-Korean words for flat and land. In native Korean the city was called Buruna or, less commonly, Barana, which may mean land of the field. Its other historic names include Ryugyong, Kisong, Hwangsong, Rakrang, Sŏgyong, Sodo, Hogyong, Changan and, under Japanese rule, Heijō. Early in the 20th century missionaries called it the Jerusalem of the East, because it was a stronghold of Protestant Christianity, especially during the Pyongyang Revival of 1907.

In 1955 archaeologists excavated prehistoric dwellings in a large ancient village at Kŭmtan-ni in the Pyongyang area, dating to the Jeulmun and Mumun pottery periods. According to legend the city was founded in 1122 BCE on the site of the capital of the traditional king Tan'gun. Korean historiography beginning with the 13th-century Samguk yusa links it to Asadal, or Wanggeom-seong, the first capital of Gojoseon. Historians reject this because earlier Chinese works such as the Records of the Grand Historian mention a much later Joseon, so the link may have been asserted by North Korea for propaganda, though Pyongyang did become a major city in old Joseon.

Wanggeom-seong, on the site of modern Pyongyang, served as the capital of Gojoseon from 194 to 108 BCE and fell in the Han conquest of 108 BCE. Emperor Wu of Han ordered four commanderies set up, with Lelang Commandery at the centre and its capital, called Joseon, at the location of Pyongyang. Pyongyang was also the capital of Goguryeo and later served as a secondary capital of Goryeo. Until 1946 it was the provincial capital of South Pyongan Province.

Pyongyang is the capital and largest city of North Korea, a directly administered city with a status equal to the provinces. It became the de facto capital after the state's founding in 1948 and was declared the official capital by the 1972 Constitution. The 2008 census counted 3,255,288 people. The city was devastated in the Korean War and quickly rebuilt with Soviet assistance. Kim Il Sung University, the country's oldest, was founded there in 1946. The best-known local dish is Pyongyang raengmyŏn, thin buckwheat noodles in a cold meat broth with watery kimchi and a slice of sweet Korean pear.
pyotr-ilyich-tchaikovsky: Tchaikovsky was born on 7 May 1840 in Votkinsk, a small town in Vyatka Governorate near the Kama River. His father, Ilya Petrovich Tchaikovsky, was a lieutenant colonel and engineer in the Department of Mines and managed the Ironworks in Kamsko-Votkinsk. Although musically precocious, he was educated for a career as a civil servant, since there was little opportunity for a musical career in Russia and no institutional music education. On 10 June 1859, aged 19, he graduated as a titular counselor, a low rung on the civil service ladder, and spent three years in the Ministry of Justice. He then entered the new Saint Petersburg Conservatory, from which he graduated in 1865.

The Western-oriented teaching he received at the conservatory set him apart from the nationalist composers of The Five, Mily Balakirev, César Cui, Modest Mussorgsky, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov and Alexander Borodin, who thought conservatories unnecessary. Tchaikovsky and his fellow students were caught between them and Anton Rubinstein, who defended professional training. His successes came infrequently and with great effort, and he was lifelong sensitive to criticism; Nikolai Rubinstein attacked the First Piano Concerto in private fits of rage. Hans von Bülow premiered it and championed other works. From 1867 the publication of his songs and piano music for the home market helped his popularity.

In March 1884 Emperor Alexander III conferred on him the Order of Saint Vladimir, which carried hereditary nobility and a personal audience with the Tsar. In 1885 the emperor requested a new production of Eugene Onegin at the Bolshoi Kamenny Theatre, signalling that his music was replacing Italian opera as the official imperial art, and awarded him a lifetime annual pension of 3,000 rubles. In his last years he grew at ease with the Belyayev circle around Rimsky-Korsakov. In 1892 he was voted a member of the Académie des Beaux-Arts in France, and in 1893 the University of Cambridge gave him an honorary Doctor of Music degree.

Tchaikovsky died in Saint Petersburg on 6 November 1893, aged 53, and was interred in Tikhvin Cemetery at the Alexander Nevsky Monastery. His death is attributed to cholera, caused by drinking unboiled water at a local restaurant. In the 1980s there was academic speculation in Britain that he killed himself, and Roland John Wiley wrote that we do not know how he died and may never find out. His music has remained popular, though critics were initially divided: some Russians thought it insufficiently Russian, while some Europeans praised it for offering more than exoticism.
pythagoras: No authentic writings of Pythagoras survive, and almost nothing is known for certain about his life. The earliest sources, from Xenophanes, Heraclitus, Empedocles, Ion of Chios and Herodotus, are brief, ambiguous and often satirical. The main biographies, by Diogenes Laërtius, Porphyry and Iamblichus, date from late antiquity and are filled with myths and legends, which grow more fantastic the later the writer.

Herodotus and Isocrates agree that Pythagoras was the son of Mnesarchus and was born on the island of Samos in the eastern Aegean. Aristoxenus stated that Pythagoras left Samos in the reign of Polycrates at the age of 40, which gives a birth date around 570 BCE. Most scholars agree that he travelled to Croton in southern Italy around 530 BCE, where he founded a school.

The teaching most securely linked to Pythagoras is metempsychosis, the belief that every soul is immortal and enters a new body after death. The earliest source is a satirical poem by Xenophanes, who describes Pythagoras interceding for a beaten dog, in whose cries he recognised the voice of a dead friend. He may also have devised the harmony of the spheres, by which the planets move according to mathematical ratios and produce an inaudible music.

The school at Croton resembled a monastery. Its members were bound by a vow to Pythagoras and each other, shared their possessions and ate meals in common. Pythagoras was credited in antiquity with the Pythagorean theorem and with discoveries in music and astronomy, but historians debate whether he made them. The geometric principles were known in Babylonian mathematics and in ancient India, and Burkert notes that antiquity never credited Pythagoras with proving any theorem.

After the decisive victory of Croton over Sybaris around 510 BCE, Pythagoras's followers came into conflict with supporters of democracy, and their meeting houses were burned. Pythagoras may have been killed in this persecution, or he may have escaped to Metapontum and died there.

Pythagoras influenced Plato, whose dialogues, especially the Timaeus, show Pythagorean ideas. His teachings revived in the first century BCE among Middle Platonists, and in the Middle Ages he was revered as the founder of mathematics and music. Nicolaus Copernicus cited Pythagoreans as influences on his heliocentric model, and Johannes Kepler, who considered himself a Pythagorean, took the title of his Harmonices Mundi from the doctrine of the harmony of the spheres.
